lessons.title: Case Study: Building an Efficient Frontier With Five Nifty 50 Stocks

children.text: Every tool from this chapter comes together here. Five real Nifty 50 stocks, spanning five different sectors, get a full covariance matrix, a minimum-variance portfolio, and a genuine efficient frontier traced out end to end, using nothing beyond what Lessons 1 through 4 already built.

body.text: A well-built efficient frontier does not just beat the worst individual stock in a universe. It beats EVERY individual stock in it, at every return level those stocks could offer. This case study shows exactly how much.

children.text: Chapter 2's four-stock universe, TCS, Maruti Suzuki, HDFC Bank, and HUL, gains a fifth name here: Reliance Industries, spanning energy, telecom, and retail. Five different sectors, five different sets of return drivers, exactly the kind of universe Chapter 1 argued for from the very first lesson.

body.code:
import numpy as np

names = ["TCS", "Maruti Suzuki", "HDFC Bank", "HUL", "Reliance Industries"]
vols = np.array([22, 28, 25, 18, 24])
expected_returns = np.array([16, 20, 17, 11, 15])
corr = np.array([
    [1.00, 0.30, 0.25, 0.10, 0.30],
    [0.30, 1.00, 0.35, 0.15, 0.25],
    [0.25, 0.35, 1.00, 0.20, 0.35],
    [0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 1.00, 0.15],
    [0.30, 0.25, 0.35, 0.15, 1.00],
])

cov_matrix = corr * np.outer(vols, vols)
ones = np.ones(5)
inv_cov = np.linalg.inv(cov_matrix)

# Minimum-variance portfolio, from Lesson 3's matrix formula
w_mv = (inv_cov @ ones) / (ones @ inv_cov @ ones)
for n, w in zip(names, w_mv):
    print(f"{n}: {w*100:.2f}%")
print(f"MV return: {w_mv @ expected_returns:.2f}%")
print(f"MV risk: {np.sqrt(w_mv @ cov_matrix @ w_mv):.2f}%")
body.caption: Same covariance-matrix-building code as Chapter 2, Lesson 3, now with a fifth stock and its expected return added.

body.label: Minimum-variance portfolio: return and risk
body.context: Lower risk than the four-stock minimum-variance portfolio from Lesson 3 (13.80%), because a fifth, only moderately correlated stock gives the optimizer one more way to cancel out risk.

body.text: HUL again takes the largest weight, 45.68%, unsurprising since it carries both the lowest individual risk (18%) and generally the lowest correlations with the other four. What is more interesting is Reliance: it does NOT have the lowest individual risk, 24% sits in the middle of the pack, yet it still earns a solid 14.18% weight. The optimizer is not rewarding low risk on its own. It is rewarding whatever combination of risk and correlation cancels out the most portfolio-level variance, and Reliance's moderate correlation with every other stock here makes it a useful diversifier even without being the calmest stock in the room.

children.text: Lesson 4's closed-form formula, solved at a sequence of target returns above the minimum-variance point, traces the frontier out point by point. Every row below still holds long-only, positive weights in all five stocks.

body.caption: The efficient frontier, five stocks, long-only

body.text: Compare the frontier to the individual stocks in the very first table of this lesson. TCS alone offers 16% return at 22% risk. The frontier hits that same 16% return at only 15.00% risk, seven full percentage points lower. HDFC Bank alone offers 17% return at 25% risk. The frontier's 17% point needs only 16.71% risk. At every return level any of these five stocks could offer on its own, the frontier delivers it for meaningfully less risk. This is not a special property of these five stocks. It is what an efficient frontier does, by construction, for any set of assets that are not perfectly correlated with each other.

By 17.50% target return, HUL's weight has fallen to just 0.8%, and it crosses zero into short territory a little past 17.6%. Beyond that point, exactly as Lesson 4 showed with four stocks, hitting a higher target return means the unconstrained optimizer wants to bet against HUL, not just hold less of it. This table stopped at 17.50% deliberately, at the edge of what a long-only investor can actually implement without a no-short-selling constraint changing the math. Chapter 6 covers what the frontier looks like once that constraint is added back in.

body.title: Price the cost of more return
body.prompt: Using this lesson's table, how many percentage points of extra risk does an investor take on, moving from the minimum-variance portfolio (13.95% return, 13.43% risk) to the 17.00% target-return portfolio (16.71% risk)?
body.explanation: 16.71% - 13.43% = 3.28 percentage points of additional risk, in exchange for 17.00% - 13.95% = 3.05 percentage points of additional expected return. Whether that trade is worth it depends entirely on the investor's own risk tolerance, which is exactly why the frontier is a menu of choices, not a single answer.

body.title: Why Reliance earns a real weight
body.question: Reliance Industries has the third-lowest individual risk (24%) among these five stocks, behind HUL (18%) and TCS (22%), yet it still receives a meaningful 14.18% weight in the minimum-variance portfolio. What best explains this?
options: The optimizer made an error; only the lowest-risk stocks should receive weight
Reliance has the highest expected return, so it is included to boost the portfolio's return
Reliance's moderate correlation with every other stock in the set makes it a useful diversifier, even though it is not individually the calmest stock
Weights in a minimum-variance portfolio are always spread evenly across all included assets
body.explanation: Minimum-variance optimization does not simply favor low individual risk. It favors whatever combination of variances and covariances cancels out the most total portfolio variance. Reliance's moderate correlation with the other four stocks earns it real weight despite not having the lowest standalone risk, exactly the covariance-driven logic Chapter 2 introduced.

cards.definition: Markowitz's 1952 framework for judging an entire portfolio's risk and return together, using expected returns, variances, and covariances.
The set of portfolios where improving expected return is only possible by accepting more risk. A curve for two assets, the upper-left boundary of a region for more.
The single lowest-risk point achievable from a given set of assets, found by w* = Sigma-inverse x 1, normalized to sum to 1.
Every efficient portfolio's weights are a linear function of its target return, so any two distinct efficient portfolios can be blended to reconstruct the entire frontier.

points: A five-stock efficient frontier, built from real sector diversity, reached a minimum-variance risk of 13.43%, lower than the four-stock version from earlier lessons, because a fifth genuinely different asset gave the optimizer more to work with.
At every return level any single stock in this universe could offer on its own, the frontier delivered the same return for noticeably less risk, by seven full points in TCS's case.

Weight in a minimum-variance portfolio is not simply a reward for low individual risk. Reliance earned a meaningful weight through moderate correlation with the other four stocks, not through being the calmest stock in the set.
The long-only frontier in this case study runs out around a 17.6% target return, past which HUL's weight would need to turn negative, a short position, exactly as Chapter 6 will address directly.

This case study closes Chapter 3's technical arc: covariance and correlation from Chapter 2 feed directly into the minimum-variance formula and the full optimization from Lessons 3 and 4, producing a complete, real efficient frontier from five ordinary Nifty 50 stocks.
Chapter 4 turns from building the frontier to using it: adding a risk-free asset, and the Capital Market Line that follows.
